scenes.title: Leaving Venice
scenes.caption: In 1271, seventeen-year-old Marco left Venice with his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo. The brothers had already been to Kublai Khan's court, and were going back with his request for a hundred learned Christians and oil from Jerusalem.

scenes.title: Across the Adriatic
scenes.caption: They sailed down the Adriatic toward the Holy Land, the usual route for Venetian merchants heading east. On a merchant ship of the time, passengers shared the deck with cargo, rope and the crew working the lateen sails.

scenes.title: The harbour at Acre
scenes.caption: Acre was the last great crusader port in the Holy Land, and the papal legate Teobaldo Visconti was there. The Polos went to him first, to ask leave to fetch the oil from Jerusalem.

scenes.title: Oil for the Khan
scenes.caption: In Jerusalem they took oil from the lamp that burned at the Holy Sepulchre. Kublai had asked for it on their first visit, and they carried it all the way to his court.

scenes.title: Letters from the legate
scenes.caption: Back in Acre, the legate gave them letters for the Khan, explaining that the Church still had no pope to send the learned men he wanted. The papal throne had then been empty for nearly three years.

scenes.title: From the port to the road
scenes.caption: At Ayas, news reached them that the legate had been elected Pope Gregory X. He called them back to Acre and sent two Dominican friars with them, but at Ayas the friars heard that the Mamluks had invaded Armenia, and turned back.

scenes.title: Carpets of Turcomania
scenes.caption: Crossing Turcomania, the Anatolian lands under Mongol rule, he wrote that the best and handsomest carpets in the world were woven there. He named Konya, Kayseri and Sivas as its chief cities.

scenes.title: Cloth at Erzincan
scenes.caption: At Arzinga, the modern Erzincan, he noted the best buckram in the world, a fine cotton cloth. The town also had hot springs, which he called the best baths anywhere.

scenes.title: Across the Armenian highlands
scenes.caption: Greater Armenia was cold, high country, where he said even the Tartar armies could not stay the winter. Passing near a great mountain, he heard that Noah's ark rested on its summit.

scenes.title: The market of Tabriz
scenes.caption: He described Tauris, now Tabriz, as a great city of trade. Goods came from India, Baghdad, Mosul and Hormuz, and Latin merchants, most of them Genoese, came to buy them.

scenes.title: Weighing a purchase
scenes.caption: Among the goods he listed at Tauris were silks, cloth of gold and precious stones. Deals like these would have been settled on a balance, with silver weighed rather than counted.

scenes.title: The tombs shown at Saveh
scenes.caption: At Saba, now Saveh, he was shown three handsome tombs said to hold the three Magi, their bodies still whole. He was told the three kings had set out from here to worship the newborn Christ.

scenes.title: Silk from Yazd
scenes.caption: He called Yazd a noble city of trade, where a silk cloth called yazdi was woven and carried to many markets. Beyond it, he wrote, the road crossed seven days of plain with only three places to stay.

scenes.title: Embroidery in Kerman
scenes.caption: At Kerman, he noted that the women embroidered silk in many colours with animals and birds of every kind, very skilfully. He also described the falcons bred in its mountains.

scenes.title: Turquoise and worked steel
scenes.caption: He recorded turquoise mined in Kerman's mountains, and veins of steel and ondanique, from which its smiths made bridles, saddles, swords and bows. Ondanique was probably a fine Indian steel.

scenes.title: Shelter after the raid
scenes.caption: Near Camadi, raiders he called Caraonas fell on the caravan, under cover of a darkness he believed they raised by magic. The Polos escaped to a village called Conosalmi; most of their companions were killed or sold as slaves.

scenes.title: Old Hormuz on the mainland
scenes.caption: In 1272 Hormuz still stood on the mainland, near the mouth of the Minab river. He found a busy port for spices, pearls and horses bound for India, but so hot that in summer people lay in water up to their necks.

scenes.title: Planks joined with cord
scenes.caption: He distrusted the local ships: their planks were sewn together with twine made from coconut husk, without iron nails, and many were lost at sea. The Polos chose not to sail for China from here.

scenes.title: Back through Kerman
scenes.caption: From Hormuz they went back to Kerman by another road, to go east overland. He wrote that the water on the way was bitter and green as grass, and drinking it brought on a flux.

scenes.title: A polished steel mirror
scenes.caption: At Cobinan, now Kuhbanan, he saw large steel mirrors of fine quality. The town also made tutty, a zinc ointment for the eyes, by heating earth in a furnace and collecting what rose from it.

scenes.title: The country of the Dry Tree
scenes.caption: Beyond the desert lay Tonocain, around the modern Tun, on a plain with a single great tree he called the Dry Tree. He wrote that Alexander had fought Darius there.

scenes.title: Melons dried for the road
scenes.caption: He called the melons of Sapurgan, now Sheberghan, the best in the world. People cut them into strips like pumpkin, dried them in the sun and sold them far and wide, sweet as honey.

scenes.title: The ruined city of Balkh
scenes.caption: He called Balkh a noble and great city, now much reduced: the Tartars had sacked it, and many of its palaces and marble houses lay in ruins. He was told that Alexander had married Darius's daughter there.

scenes.title: Salt from the mountains
scenes.caption: Near Taican, now Taloqan, he saw mountains made of salt, so hard it had to be dug with iron picks. He thought there was enough to supply the whole world until the end of time.

scenes.title: A pause in Badakhshan
scenes.caption: Marco fell ill in Badakhshan and stayed about a year. He was advised to go up into the mountains, and the clean air there cured him.

scenes.title: Lapis and balas rubies
scenes.caption: Badakhshan's mines yielded balas rubies and the finest lapis lazuli. Only the king could dig the rubies, and anyone caught taking them out of the country risked death.

scenes.title: Up the Wakhan valley
scenes.caption: From Badakhshan the road ran twelve days up the Oxus into Vokhan, now the Wakhan. He noted that its people had a language of their own and were brave fighters.

scenes.title: Crossing the high plain
scenes.caption: Beyond the Wakhan the road climbed for three days to the Pamir, which he was told was the highest place in the world. For twelve days there was no dwelling, and fire burned so weakly that food would not cook properly.

scenes.title: The sheep with great horns
scenes.caption: On the Pamir he saw great wild sheep whose horns were up to six palms long; shepherds made bowls from them. The Pamir argali is now named Ovis ammon polii, Marco Polo's sheep.

scenes.title: Gardens around Kashgar
scenes.caption: After the mountains came Kashgar, which he described as a land of gardens, vineyards and fine estates, growing cotton, flax and hemp. Its merchants travelled the world, and Nestorian Christians lived among the Muslims.

scenes.title: Water in the oasis
scenes.caption: At Yarcan, now Yarkand, he wrote that many people had swollen legs or goitres, which he blamed on the water they drank. The oasis lived on its irrigation channels and gardens.

scenes.title: Searching the riverbed
scenes.caption: He described Khotan as a well-supplied province of cotton, flax, hemp and grain, its people traders and craftsmen. He did not mention its jade, which had gone from these riverbeds to China for more than a thousand years.

scenes.title: A handful of jade
scenes.caption: Khotan's jade is nephrite, found as rounded pebbles in the White Jade and Black Jade rivers. Worked by grinding with abrasive sand, it had reached Chinese courts for more than a thousand years before Polo passed.

scenes.title: Stones from the Keriya waters
scenes.caption: At Pem, probably near modern Keriya, he noted jasper and chalcedony in the rivers. He also recorded that a wife whose husband was away more than twenty days could take another husband.

scenes.title: A settlement at the sand's edge
scenes.caption: Charchan, now Qiemo, was a sandy province, and he noted jasper and chalcedony carried from its rivers to China. When an army came through, people fled two or three days into the sand with their animals, to places where they knew of water.

scenes.title: Provisioning at Lop
scenes.caption: Lop was the last town before the desert. Travellers rested there a week, then loaded a month's food for themselves and their animals: crossing the desert even at its narrowest, he said, took a month.

scenes.title: Keeping together after dark
scenes.caption: He reported that spirits in the desert called travellers by name, so that anyone who fell behind was lost. Caravans kept close together at night and hung bells on their animals so that no one would stray.

scenes.title: Paper figures at Dunhuang
scenes.caption: At Sachiu, now Dunhuang, he described funerals at which paper figures of men, horses and camels, and paper coins, were burned with the dead. People believed these would serve them in the next world.

scenes.title: Rhubarb for distant markets
scenes.caption: In the mountains of Succiu, now Jiuquan, he wrote, the finest rhubarb grew, and merchants carried it from there all over the world. Dried rhubarb root was a prized medicine as far away as Europe.

scenes.title: A reclining Buddha at Ganzhou
scenes.caption: The Polos spent a year at Campichu, now Zhangye, on business he did not explain. He described great monasteries with lying idols ten paces long; one such reclining Buddha, made around 1098, still lies in Zhangye's Great Buddha Temple.

scenes.title: A shaggy pack animal
scenes.caption: Around Ergiuul, now Wuwei, he described wild cattle as big as elephants, with long silky hair, and tame ones bred from them: yaks. He also brought the dried head and feet of a musk deer home to Venice.

scenes.title: Cloth from camel hair
scenes.caption: At Egrigaia, now Yinchuan, he praised the camlets woven from camel hair, the finest in the world, some of them white. Merchants carried them to Cathay and beyond.

scenes.title: A Christian community on the steppe
scenes.caption: At Tenduc, he wrote, the ruler was a Christian named George, of the Önggüt, whom he took for a descendant of Prester John. The Önggüt really were Christians of the Church of the East, and Chinese records name this prince Körgüz.

scenes.title: Birds by the lake
scenes.caption: At Chagannor, the Khan had a palace beside a lake full of swans, cranes and other birds. He came there to hunt with gyrfalcons and hawks, and had millet sown along the shores so the birds would have food.

scenes.title: The summer capital
scenes.caption: In 1275 the Polos reached Kublai at Shangdu, his summer capital, more than three years after leaving Venice. The Khan had sent riders forty days' journey out to meet them.

scenes.title: The palace of cane
scenes.caption: Inside Shangdu's park stood a palace of cane, gilded and lacquered, that could be taken apart and moved. He wrote that more than two hundred silk cords held it up against the wind.

scenes.title: An audience with Kublai
scenes.caption: The Polos knelt before Kublai and gave him the Pope's letters and the oil from Jerusalem, and Niccolò presented his son. The Khan welcomed Marco and took him into his household.

scenes.title: Streets of the new capital
scenes.caption: Kublai's new capital, Dadu, which Polo called Khanbaliq, was laid out on a grid, its streets so straight that one could see from gate to gate. He wrote that the whole city was planned like a chessboard.

scenes.title: Paper accepted as money
scenes.caption: He was amazed that the Khan's subjects accepted paper money, made from mulberry bark and stamped with the Khan's red seal. Anyone who forged it, he wrote, was put to death.

scenes.title: Fresh horses at a post station
scenes.caption: He described the Khan's post roads, with stations every twenty-five or thirty miles keeping hundreds of horses ready. Riders changing horses at each station could carry a message more than two hundred miles in a day.

scenes.title: The bridge and its stone lions
scenes.caption: Ten miles from the capital he crossed a marble bridge over a river he called Pulisanghin, Persian for 'stone bridge', with carved lions along its parapets. He counted twenty-four arches; the Lugou Bridge has eleven, and English speakers still call it the Marco Polo Bridge.

scenes.title: Where the roads divide
scenes.caption: A little beyond the bridge was Juju, now Zhuozhou, where, he wrote, the roads parted. One ran west through Cathay toward Tibet and Yunnan; the other ran south-east to Manzi, the former Song lands.

scenes.title: Silk in Hejian
scenes.caption: Going south toward Manzi, he passed Cacanfu, now Hejian, a city that made silk and cloth of silk and gold. He noted a church of Nestorian Christians there.

scenes.title: Drawing salt from the earth
scenes.caption: At Cianglu, now Changlu, he watched salt made from the earth: people heaped up salty soil, poured water over it, and collected the brine that drained out. The Changlu salt works remained among China's largest for centuries.

scenes.title: Crystals in the salt pan
scenes.caption: The brine was then boiled in great iron pans until the salt crystallised, white and fine. He noted that the trade brought the Khan a large revenue.

scenes.title: A waterway joining north and south
scenes.caption: At Sinjumatu, now Jining, he saw a river divided in two, one half flowing north toward Cathay and the other south toward Manzi. This was the summit of the Grand Canal, where Kublai's engineers were cutting new channels to carry grain to the capital.

scenes.title: Crossing into Manzi
scenes.caption: He crossed the Caramoran, the Mongols' 'Black River', as he called the Yellow River, which then reached the sea by way of the Huai. On the far bank lay Coiganju, now Huai'an, the gateway to Manzi.

scenes.title: Fish beside the canal
scenes.caption: At Cayu, now Gaoyou, the road ran along a stone causeway beside the canal, through wide water and marsh. He noted fish and game in great abundance.

scenes.title: Merchants at Yangzhou
scenes.caption: Yangiu, now Yangzhou, was a great city ruling twenty-seven others, and he claimed to have governed it for three years on the Khan's orders. No Chinese record mentions him, and many scholars think he held a lesser post, perhaps in the salt administration.

scenes.title: A Christian church at Zhenjiang
scenes.caption: At Chinghianfu, now Zhenjiang, he found two Nestorian churches built in 1278 by Mar Sargis, a Christian whom the Khan had made governor. A Chinese gazetteer of about 1333 confirms him, and credits him with seven churches, six of them around the city.

scenes.title: A bridge in Suzhou
scenes.caption: He described Suju, now Suzhou, as a very great city with six thousand stone bridges, high enough for a galley to pass under. Its people lived by trade and crafts.

scenes.title: Choosing a length of silk
scenes.caption: So much silk was made around Suzhou, he wrote, that everyone was dressed in it, and great quantities went to market. He noted that its merchants were rich, but not men of war.

scenes.title: Waterways of Hangzhou
scenes.caption: He called Quinsay, now Hangzhou, 'beyond dispute the finest and noblest city in the world'. Its name came from xingzai, the 'temporary capital' of the fallen Song, and he counted twelve thousand bridges over its canals.

scenes.title: A southern market
scenes.caption: He described ten great market squares in Quinsay, each holding a market three days a week for forty or fifty thousand people. He listed fish brought fresh from the sea every day, game, and pears weighing ten pounds each.

scenes.title: Boats on the lake
scenes.caption: On West Lake, he wrote, pleasure boats with tables and painted cabins carried parties of friends, who could see the whole city and its palaces from the water. Fine houses and Buddhist monasteries stood all around the shore.

scenes.title: Toward the Fujian hills
scenes.caption: From Quinsay the road south ran up into hill country, through towns he called Vuju and Ghiuju, now Wuzhou and Quzhou. He noted prosperous towns, plenty of silk, and canes of great size along the way.

scenes.title: The chickens with soft plumage
scenes.caption: At Quenlinfu, now Jian'ou, he noted handsome stone bridges, ginger and galingale. He also described hens with no feathers, only a coat like a cat's fur: the breed now called the silkie.

scenes.title: Sugar for trade
scenes.caption: He described Fuju, now Fuzhou, as a great trading city, where ships brought pearls and precious stones from India, and sugar was made in enormous quantities. Nearby, he said, men from 'Babylon', meaning Egypt, had taught the people to refine it.

scenes.title: The port of Zaiton
scenes.caption: He called Zaiton, now Quanzhou, one of the two greatest ports in the world. For every shipload of pepper that went to Alexandria for Christendom, he wrote, a hundred came to Zaiton.

scenes.title: Loading for the voyage
scenes.caption: Kublai fitted out fourteen four-masted ships for the princess's voyage, some with crews of two hundred and fifty. He had them provisioned, Polo wrote, for two years at sea.

scenes.title: The princess's escort
scenes.caption: In 1291 the Polos sailed with Kököchin, a seventeen-year-old Mongol princess sent as a bride to the Ilkhan Arghun. A Yuan post-station record of 1290, found by Yang Zhijiu in 1941, names her three Persian envoys exactly as Polo does: Uladai, Abishqa and Khoja.

scenes.title: Along the coast of Champa
scenes.caption: The fleet coasted south to Ciamba, the kingdom of Champa, which Marco had visited in 1285. Its king paid the Khan tribute in elephants and aloes-wood, and had, he said, 326 children.

scenes.title: Sondur and Condur
scenes.caption: Past Champa, he noted two islands he called Sondur and Condur, now the Côn Sơn islands. Later sailors knew them as Pulo Condore, a landmark on the route between China and the Malay world.

scenes.title: Feeling a way through the shallows
scenes.caption: Near Pentam, now Bintan, he wrote, the sea between the islands was so shallow, only four paces deep, that ships had to draw up their rudders. Beyond lay the strait leading to Sumatra.

scenes.title: Waiting for the monsoon
scenes.caption: The fleet waited five months at Samara, on Sumatra, for the monsoon to turn. The party built a timber stockade against the man-eaters they had heard lived inland, and traded with the islanders for food.

scenes.title: The anchorage in rain
scenes.caption: He called Sumatra 'Java the Less', and noted that from here the Pole Star could no longer be seen. He described the palm wine drawn from cut branches, and the sago flour of the neighbouring kingdom of Fansur.

scenes.title: Coconuts on an island shore
scenes.caption: Sailing north-west, they passed Necuveram, the Nicobar Islands, where he said people went naked and had no king. He listed red sandalwood, coconuts and brazilwood among its trees.

scenes.title: Stones from Seilan
scenes.caption: He wrote that Seilan, Sri Lanka, produced the finest rubies in the world, and that its king owned one a palm long, flawless and red as fire. Kublai, he said, had offered a city for it and been refused.

scenes.title: The pearl fishery
scenes.caption: In Maabar, on the Gulf of Mannar, he described pearl divers going down from boats into four to twelve fathoms of water. They paid a tenth to the king and a share to the Brahmins who charmed the sharks so they would not attack.

scenes.title: Sorting the catch
scenes.caption: He wrote that the king of Maabar wore a necklace of 104 large pearls and rubies, one for each prayer he said every day. The king allowed no large pearls to leave his kingdom.

scenes.title: Rounding the southern cape
scenes.caption: At Comari, Cape Comorin, he saw the Pole Star again for the first time since Java, just above the horizon. From here the ships turned north up the Malabar coast.

scenes.title: Pepper at Quilon
scenes.caption: At Coilum, now Kollam, he described pepper gathered in May, June and July from vines planted and watered like crops. He also noted brazilwood and the best indigo, made from a herb soaked in water and dried in the sun.

scenes.title: Landfall in Persia
scenes.caption: After eighteen months at sea the fleet reached Hormuz. Of some six hundred people who had sailed, he wrote, only eighteen survived, among them the princess and one of the three envoys.

scenes.title: Tablets for the road west
scenes.caption: Arghun had died, so the princess was married to his son Ghazan. The new Ilkhan Gaykhatu gave the Polos four golden tablets of authority, and while they were in Persia news came that Kublai himself had died.

scenes.title: Reduced baggage at Trebizond
scenes.caption: At Trebizond, on the Black Sea, the Polos were robbed of part of their goods. Fifteen years later, Maffeo's will still recorded the property taken from them in the empire of Trebizond.

scenes.title: Through the Bosporus
scenes.caption: From Trebizond they sailed along the Black Sea to Constantinople, where the Venetians had their own quarter. The book says almost nothing about this last stage; Marco was nearly home.

scenes.title: The narrow channel at Negroponte
scenes.caption: On the way home they called at Negroponte, the Venetian port on Euboea, beside the narrow Euripus strait. From here Venetian ships followed the coasts of Greece and Dalmatia up to Venice.

scenes.title: Venice after twenty-four years
scenes.caption: They reached Venice in 1295, twenty-four years after leaving; Marco was about forty-one. A story first printed in 1559 says even their relatives did not know them until they slit open their old coats and jewels spilled out.

scenes.title: What came home
scenes.caption: The book says they came home rich, and Venetian documents show Marco as a prosperous merchant for the rest of his life. In his will of 1324 he freed his servant Peter, 'of the Tartar race'.

scenes.title: The journey becomes a book
scenes.caption: Captured by the Genoese, perhaps at the battle of Curzola in 1298, he dictated his travels in prison to a fellow captive, the romance writer Rustichello of Pisa. On his deathbed, urged to take back its marvels, he is said to have replied that he had not told half of what he saw.
